patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent brief episodes of eyelid fluttering and unresponsiveness — 3 months, frequency increasing
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. D is a 35-year-old marketing manager who presents with 3-month history of recurrent brief episodes of bilateral eyelid fluttering and unresponsiveness. The episodes last 20-40 seconds each, occur up to 10 times per day at their worst, and have been increasing in frequency over the past month. Her husband, who has witnessed most episodes, describes them as occurring suddenly, with bilateral eyelid flutter (described as rapid blinking), slight head turning to the right, brief unresponsiveness with no ability to respond to questions, followed by immediate and complete recovery with no post-event confusion. She reports that the episodes are sometimes triggered by stress and occasionally by bright lights. She has not been injured during an episode. She has a history of febrile convulsions at age 3 (resolved) and her maternal aunt has adult-onset epilepsy treated with levetiracetam. She was started on escitalopram for anxiety approximately 8 months ago with good effect. The episodes began coincidentally approximately 3 months ago during a period of intense work stress following her promotion to marketing director, coinciding with her husband's prostate cancer diagnosis. She has not had a prior EEG. She is extremely worried that she has epilepsy given her family history and childhood febrile seizures. She denies any tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-ictal confusion with any of the episodes.

findings.type: Episode of eyelid flutter and unresponsiveness — 32 seconds
findings.morphology: NO EEG CHANGE during entire episode. Normal continuous background. CRITICALLY: absence seizures characteristically produce bilateral 3 Hz spike-and-wave during clinical event. NO spike-and-wave observed. The clinical eyelid flutter is NOT accompanied by EEG correlate. This definitively excludes typical absence seizures.

findings.morphology: No EEG change during hyperventilation provocation. No spike-wave activation. In childhood/adult absence epilepsy, hyperventilation reliably provokes 3 Hz spike-wave bursts — negative provocation test is further evidence against absence epilepsy.

results.title: Distinguishing PNES from absence seizures: clinical and EEG features

output.summary: PNES can closely mimic absence seizures clinically but are reliably distinguished by video-EEG: absence seizures invariably produce bilateral 3 Hz spike-wave during every single event without exception. Negative hyperventilation provocation and negative EEG during events definitively exclude absence epilepsy. PNES mimicking absence seizures are not rare and are diagnosed in approximately 20% of patients referred for adult absence epilepsy workup.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Episode frequency at 4 weeks 2-3/week (from 10/day at admission) episodes/week (H).

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — PNES mimicking absence seizures

differential.key_feature: Video-EEG during clinical event shows NO 3 Hz spike-wave discharge — absence seizures INVARIABLY produce this on EVERY event without exception; negative hyperventilation provocation further excludes absence epilepsy
Normal MRI with no mesial temporal sclerosis; EEG shows no focal temporal changes; partial responsiveness during event could suggest focal awareness but EEG excludes focal epileptic activity
No morning myoclonic jerks; EEG normal without polyspike activity; age of onset and pattern inconsistent
SSRIs can rarely lower seizure threshold but would produce EEG changes; EEG is normal; episodes began before any dose change

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain — exclude structural epilepsy cause (mesial temporal sclerosis, dysplasia)
Video-EEG with hyperventilation provocation and event capture
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No 3 Hz spike-wave during event or hyperventilation — absence epilepsy excluded; PNES confirmed
Moderate anxiety and depression; identified work/family stressors

optimal_actions.action: FND treatment: CBT and explain diagnosis to patient

critical_actions: Video-EEG with event capture — absence seizures have invariable 3 Hz spike-wave on EVERY event
Do not prescribe AEDs without EEG confirmation of epilepsy
Family history of epilepsy and childhood febrile convulsions increase patient's anxiety but do not confirm epilepsy
contraindicated_actions: Prescribing valproate or ethosuximide without EEG confirmation of absence epilepsy
Telling patient the episodes are 'nothing' — they are real and distressing
key_reasoning_points: KEY: Absence seizures produce bilateral 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharge during EVERY SINGLE CLINICAL EVENT without exception — this is pathognomonic. Normal EEG during clinical eyelid flutter definitively excludes absence epilepsy.
Hyperventilation provocation reliably activates absence seizure EEG in absence epilepsy patients — negative test provides additional exclusion
Partial responsiveness during event is inconsistent with typical absence seizures (which have complete unresponsiveness with stereotyped automatisms)
Childhood febrile convulsions do NOT increase risk for PNES specifically but do create valid patient concern about epilepsy that must be addressed

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history raises clinical suspicion but cannot diagnose epilepsy; video-EEG with event capture is required and definitively shows no EEG correlate — PNES confirmed

metadata.notes: Moderate FND — PNES mimicking absence seizures. Critical teaching: absence seizures have invariable 3 Hz spike-wave on video-EEG. Family epilepsy history is a red herring.
